definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia, the paired skin folds surrounding the vaginal opening; used in medical and educational contexts.
notes: Composed of 阴 (yin/female/genital) + 唇 (lip); the collective term covering both labia majora and minora when unspecified.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia majora, the outer pair of skin folds forming the outer boundary of the vulva.
notes: Literally 'big yin-lips'; standard anatomical term in Chinese medical education; lower recognition than 阴唇 due to anatomical specificity.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the labia minora, the inner pair of skin folds surrounding the vaginal opening and urethral meatus.
notes: Literally 'small yin-lips'; paired anatomical term with 大阴唇; recognition is lower than the collective term 阴唇.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the mons pubis, the fatty tissue mound over the pubic symphysis; rarely encountered outside medical contexts.
notes: Composed of 阴 (yin/female) + 阜 (mound/hillock); a low-frequency anatomical term not widely known among the general public; poor sex education in China depresses lay recognition of sub-labia anatomical terms.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the hymen; literally 'virgin membrane,' embedding the virginity concept directly into the anatomical name.
notes: Literally 'virgin film/membrane' (处女 = virgin + 膜 = membrane); the etymology encodes cultural obsession with female virginity into the anatomical terminology itself, unlike the neutral Latin-derived English 'hymen'; extraordinarily high recognition relative to most anatomical terms due to the heavy cultural weight placed on female virginity in Chinese society.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the vaginal opening, the external entrance to the vaginal canal.
notes: Composed of 阴道 (vaginal canal) + 口 (opening/mouth); the 口 (mouth) component is widely used in Chinese anatomical terminology for tubular openings; standard term in gynecological and sex-education contexts.

definition: The most common and versatile crude Mandarin slang for the female genitalia (vulva/vagina); functions as both anatomical descriptor and general insult.
notes: Phonetically identical to the dedicated character 屄; because 屄 is blocked by content filters, the common character 逼 (to press/force) is used as a homophonic substitute in writing; ubiquitous in internet slang, insults, and casual crude speech; arguably the single most important vulgar word in Mandarin.

definition: The dedicated Chinese character for the female genitalia; the most morphologically explicit and taboo anatomical character in the Chinese writing system.
notes: One of a small set of dedicated 'dirty characters' (秽字) in Chinese orthography; the character structure is iconically anatomical; routinely blocked by content filters, search engines, and social media platforms, driving users to write 逼 as a substitute; recognition is high among literate adults but the character almost never appears in standard published text.

definition: Crude slang for the vagina, literally 'cave' or 'hole'; the second most prevalent crude vagina term after 逼, especially common in erotic fiction.
notes: Primary meaning is 'cave,' 'acupoint,' or 'hollow'; because the character has abundant non-sexual meanings, content filters catch it less reliably than 屄, making it popular in online erotic writing; often appears in compounds such as 小穴 or 嫩穴 (tender hole).

definition: Crude compound slang for the vagina, literally 'little hole'; the dominant term for vagina in Chinese-language pornographic writing and erotic fiction.
notes: The diminutive 小 (little) adds an infantilizing or affectionate register typical of Chinese erotic discourse; this compound is overwhelmingly the most frequent vagina-slang in published erotic fiction on Chinese platforms.

definition: Extremely vulgar compound meaning 'lewd/smelly cunt'; functions both as a crude anatomical descriptor and as a highly offensive insult directed at women.
notes: 骚 (sāo) means sexually wanton, lewd, or emitting a fishy/musky odor; the compound insult is used primarily against women; in erotic contexts it describes the vulva approvingly or dismissively depending on register; equivalent in offense level to the most severe English genital insults.

definition: Universal deictic euphemism for the genitals, literally 'that place' or 'down there'; used to avoid naming genitals directly in polite or mixed company.
notes: Applies to both male and female genitalia depending on context; the most common avoidance strategy across all age groups; used in mainstream media, medical advice columns, and everyday conversation; southern Mandarin speakers may use 那里 (nàlǐ) as a regional variant.

definition: Infantilizing euphemism for the female genitalia, literally 'little sister'; used primarily when discussing female anatomy with or among young children.
notes: The corresponding male euphemism is 小弟弟 (xiǎo dìdi, 'little brother') for the penis; widely used in parent-child contexts and early sex education; the same phrase appears in erotic writing with a fetishizing infantilizing tone, creating a stark register split between innocent child-directed usage and explicit adult usage.

definition: Gender-neutral euphemism for the genitals, literally 'private place'; the dominant polite term in health journalism, sex education, and everyday conversation.
notes: Standard term in Chinese sex-education curricula, medical advice media, and news reporting on sexual assault; applies to both male and female anatomy; preferred over clinical terms in non-clinical written Chinese because it is simultaneously informative and inoffensive.

definition: Crude slang for the vulva, literally 'slit,' 'crack,' or 'seam'; refers to the external cleft appearance of the female genitalia.
notes: Primary meaning is 'seam,' 'crack,' or 'gap'; the sexual meaning is understood contextually by most adults; appears in erotic writing and crude speech; less common than 逼 or 穴 but widely recognized; less taboo than those terms because the character has abundant non-sexual meanings.

definition: Crude slang for the vagina, literally 'hole' or 'cave'; emphasizes the penetrable orifice rather than external anatomy.
notes: Primary meaning is 'cave,' 'hole,' or 'tunnel' in everyday language; in sexual slang specifically implies the vagina as a receptive orifice; somewhat less taboo than 穴 because 洞 is even more multipurpose in standard usage; also used crudely for the anus in some sexual contexts.

definition: Indirect slang for the female genitalia using the fish as a metaphor, drawing on a cross-cultural olfactory association between fish odor and vaginal secretions.
notes: The fish-vagina association appears cross-culturally; used in Chinese internet slang and regional crude expressions; recognition as a sexual metaphor is lower than 逼 or 穴 because it requires cultural context to decode; the metaphor can be used approvingly or derogatorily depending on speaker intent.

definition: Slang for the female genitalia using 'cat' as a metaphor, directly analogous to English 'pussy'; recognition has grown with exposure to English internet culture.
notes: Directly parallels the English 'pussy' slang metaphor; usage has increased among younger internet-literate speakers who consume English-language content; less dominant than 逼 or 穴 in native Mandarin erotic writing but growing in currency among younger cohorts.

definition: Literary and erotic euphemism for the female genitalia, using 'flower' as a metaphor for the vulva; rooted in classical Chinese erotic poetry and prose.
notes: The flower metaphor for female genitalia has deep roots in Ming and Qing dynasty erotic literature; in modern usage it appears primarily in literary or softcore romantic-erotic writing; far less charged than crude slang terms; recognition as a sexual metaphor among younger speakers may be declining as classical-erotic literacy decreases.

definition: The standard clinical Mandarin term for the clitoris; used in medical, anatomical, and formal sex-education contexts.
notes: Composed of 阴 (yin/female/genital) + 蒂 (stalk/stem of a fruit or flower); historically poor clitoral sex education in China has suppressed lay recognition of this term relative to comparable anatomical terms; awareness has risen with online feminist health discourse since roughly 2015.

definition: The most widely recognized non-clinical Mandarin term for the clitoris, literally 'little bean'; the dominant lay term used in health communication, feminist media, and everyday conversation.
notes: The bean metaphor refers to the rounded shape of the clitoral glans; recognition significantly exceeds that of the clinical term 阴蒂 because of its accessible, non-threatening register; prominently used in Chinese feminist online communities, mainstream media health segments, and women's magazines; 'little bean' clitoris metaphors also appear in Japanese and other East Asian lay discourse.

definition: Shortened form of 小豆豆; casual slang for the clitoris using the 'bean' shape metaphor; slightly less frequent than the full 小豆豆 form.
notes: Functionally interchangeable with 小豆豆; the doubling of 豆 maintains a playful, cutesy register; also doubles as a common personal nickname and general diminutive for small round objects, giving it plausible deniability in ambiguous contexts.

definition: Crude compound slang for the clitoris, literally 'little meat bean'; more explicitly anatomical than 小豆豆 by inserting 肉 (flesh/meat).
notes: Less common than 小豆豆 in mainstream usage; the addition of 肉 (flesh) makes the term more graphically anatomical and shifts it toward a crude register; found primarily in erotic fiction and pornographic writing rather than health communication; recognition is lower because it lacks the mainstream feminist and health-media context that boosted 小豆豆.

definition: The standard clinical and colloquial Mandarin term for the anus; used in medical, hygiene, and everyday contexts with relatively low taboo.
notes: Composed of 肛 (a dedicated character for the anus) + 门 (gate/door); unusually high recognition for a clinical anatomical term because it appears routinely in digestive health, hygiene, and toilet-training contexts; significantly less taboo in Chinese than comparable genital terms, likely because it is associated more with digestion than sexuality in standard discourse.

definition: Clinical Mandarin term for the rectum, the terminal section of the large intestine leading to the anal canal.
notes: Literally 'straight intestine'; 直肠子 (one who speaks bluntly and thoughtlessly) is a common Mandarin idiom etymologically derived from this term but carrying no sexual meaning; the clinical anatomical term appears in colorectal cancer awareness, gastroenterological contexts, and is relevant to discussions of anal sex; lower recognition than 肛门 due to greater anatomical specificity.
